                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    • Friendly is an adjective describing someone who is kind, pleasant, or amicable. While it is a positive trait, it does not specifically mean excessive praise.
                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    • Cruelty refers to behavior that causes pain or suffering to others. It is a negative trait and serves as a contextual opposite to kindness, rather than a synonym for flattery.
                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    \n
                                                                                                                                                    Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                    \n
                                                                                                                                                      \n
                                                                                                                                                    • Synonyms for Flattery include Sycophancy, Blandishment, Cajolery, and Fawning.
                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    • Antonyms for Flattery include Criticism, Condemnation, Insult, and Denunciation.
                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    • The word Adulation is derived from the Latin 'adulatio', which historically suggested the fawning behavior of a dog toward its master.
                                                                                                                                                      • \n
                                                                                                                                                    • In literature and psychology, excessive Flattery is often associated with Narcissism or Manipulative behavior.

(अस्वीकार / खंडन)\n
                                                                                                                                                          \n
                                                                                                                                                        • Example: His denial of any involvement in the crime was questioned by the police.
                                                                                                                                                          • \n
                                                                                                                                                        \n
                                                                                                                                                        • \n

(पुष्टि / समर्थन)\n
                                                                                                                                                          \n
                                                                                                                                                        • Example: The positive test results were an affirmation of the new medical treatment effectiveness.
                                                                                                                                                          • \n
                                                                                                                                                        \n

                                                                                                                                                      • Hence, we can infer that the opposite of 'Denial' is 'Affirmation'.

                                                                                                                                                      Therefore, the correct answer is: Affirmation.

                                                                                                                                                      \n\n

                                                                                                                                                      Additional Information

                                                                                                                                                      \n

                                                                                                                                                        • \n
                                                                                                                                                      • Confirm: Originates from the Latin confirmare, meaning to make firm or strengthen. It is often used in business contexts like confirming an appointment or confirming a flight.
                                                                                                                                                        • \n
                                                                                                                                                      • Conform: Originates from the Latin conformare, meaning to form or shape.                                                                                                                                                         • \n
                                                                                                                                                      • To remember the difference: Confirm has the word firm in it—you are making a fact or a plan firm. Conform is about the form or shape you take to fit in with others.
                                                                                                                                                        • \n

                                                                                                                                                Key Points
                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                • The original segment will teaches is grammatically incorrect because modal auxiliary verbs (such as will, can, could, should, may, etc.) must always be followed by the base form (V1) of the verb.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • The verb teaches is the third-person singular form; the correct base form after a modal is teach.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • Can teach is the most appropriate substitution here as it indicates the ability or proficiency of the younger brother to handle graduate students.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • Option 1 (will teach) is grammatically correct in structure, but can is often preferred in English proficiency tests to emphasize capability in a specific professional or academic context.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • Option 3 (could teach) expresses past ability or conditional possibility, which does not fit the straightforward statement of fact in the sentence.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • Option 4 (would have teach) is grammatically flawed because the phrase would have must be followed by the past participle (V3) form of the verb, which is taught.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                • Modal Verbs do not change their form based on the subject (singular or plural). For example, we say 'He can' and 'They can', never 'He cans'.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • The base form is the simplest form of a verb without any suffixes like -s, -ed, or -ing.
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • In the sentence structure Subject + Modal + Verb, the verb acts as the bare infinitive (infinitive without 'to').
                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                • Examples of correct usage: 'He can swim', 'They will arrive', 'She must study'.

                                                                                                                                                                The correct answer is Rohan keeps the keys on the table.

                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                Key Points
                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                • The given sentence is in the Passive Voice. We need to convert it into the Active Voice.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • The structure of the given passive sentence is: Object + is/am/are + V3 (past participle) + by + Subject.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • The use of are kept clearly indicates that the sentence is in the Simple Present Tense.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • To convert a Simple Present passive sentence into active voice, the structure used is: Subject + V1 (s/es) + Object.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • In the passive sentence, the keys is the grammatical subject (but the receiver of the action) and Rohan is the agent (the doer). In the active voice, Rohan moves to the subject position.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Since Rohan is a singular third-person noun, the base verb keep must take the suffix s, resulting in keeps.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Thus, the active form is: Rohan keeps the keys on the table.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Voice Transformation: In English grammar, the voice of a verb describes the relationship between the action and the participants (subject or object).
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Active Voice: The subject performs the action (e.g., Rohan keeps...).
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Passive Voice: The subject undergoes the action (e.g., The keys are kept...).
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Rules for other Tenses:
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Simple Past: Active (V2) → Passive (was/were + V3). Example: Rohan kept the keys → The keys were kept by Rohan.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Present Continuous: Active (is/am/are + V1+ing) → Passive (is/am/are + being + V3). Example: Rohan is keeping the keys → The keys are being kept by Rohan.
                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                • Present Perfect: Active (has/have + V3) → Passive (has/have + been + V3). Example: Rohan has kept the keys → The keys have been kept by Rohan.

                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                  Key Points
                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                    \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • The given sentence is in the Passive Voice and the tense used is the Present Continuous Tense.
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • The structure of Passive Voice for Present Continuous is: Object + am/is/are + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + Subject.
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • The structure of Active Voice for Present Continuous is: Subject + am/is/are + Present Participle (Verb+ing) + Object.
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • In the passive sentence, The furniture is the object and workers is the agent (logical subject).
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • To convert it to active voice:\n
                                                                                                                                                                      \n
                                                                                                                                                                    1. The agent workers becomes the subject.
                                                                                                                                                                      2. \n
                                                                                                                                                                    2. Since workers is plural, we use the auxiliary verb are.
                                                                                                                                                                      3. \n
                                                                                                                                                                    3. The verb being shifted changes to its active form shifting.
                                                                                                                                                                      4. \n
                                                                                                                                                                    4. The subject the furniture becomes the object.
                                                                                                                                                                      5. \n
                                                                                                                                                                    \n
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • Therefore, the sentence becomes: Workers are shifting the furniture to the other block.
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n

                                                                                                                                                                  • Option 3 is incorrect because it uses the Past Continuous Tense (were shifting).
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • Option 4 is incorrect because it uses the Present Perfect Tense (have shifted).
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                  Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                                  \n

                                                                                                                                                                    • \n

                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • If the subject in the Active Voice is vague or unknown (like 'someone', 'people', 'they'), it is often omitted in the Passive Voice.
                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                  • Present Continuous transformations always involve the word being in the passive form to indicate the ongoing nature of the action.

                                                                                                                                                                              • \n

                                                                                                                                                                            • 'Started working energetically' refers to beginning a task or responsibility with a lot of vigor, power, and active effort. (ऊर्जा के साथ काम शुरू किया)\n
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                              • Example: After the morning meeting, the developers started working energetically on the new software update.
                                                                                                                                                                                • \n
                                                                                                                                                                              \n
                                                                                                                                                                              • \n
                                                                                                                                                                            • Hence, the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom is to have started working energetically.
                                                                                                                                                                              • \n

                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                              Key Points
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                              • Indirect Speech: The man asked if I did not realize how serious this was.
                                                                                                                                                                                • \n
                                                                                                                                                                              • Key Conversions:\n
                                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Reporting Verb: The direct speech verb 'said' is changed to 'asked' because the sentence inside the quotation marks is an interrogative sentence (a question).
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Conjunction: For Yes/No questions (questions starting with auxiliary verbs like 'do'), the conjunction 'if' or 'whether' is used to join the reporting clause with the reported speech.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Tense Change:\n
                                                                                                                                                                                    \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  • The Present Simple negative 'do not realize' is converted into the Past Simple negative 'did not realize'.
                                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  • The verb 'is' in the subordinate clause is changed to 'was' to maintain tense consistency with the past reporting verb.
                                                                                                                                                                                    • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Pronoun Change: The second-person pronoun 'you' is changed to the first-person 'I' (assuming the man is addressing the speaker).
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Sentence Structure: In Indirect Speech, the interrogative form (verb before subject) is changed into the assertive form (subject before verb). Hence, 'do you not realize' becomes 'I did not realize'.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • \n
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                              Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                              Correct Sentence: 'The man asked if I did not realize how serious this was.'
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                              Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                                              \n\n
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                              • Option 2: 'The man asked me did I not realize how serious it was.' \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  \n

                                                                                                                                                                                The correct answer is in layman's terms

                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                                Key Points
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • The phrase 'in layman's terms' is a fixed idiomatic expression in English. It is the most suitable replacement because it is the standard way to describe explaining complex, technical, or scientific information so that a non-expert can understand it.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • A layman (or layperson) is someone who does not have specialized training or professional knowledge in a particular field, such as science, law, or medicine.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • While the original phrase 'layman's language' is understandable, 'layman's terms' is the preferred collocation used in professional and academic writing.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Option 1 ('in the language of layman') is grammatically incorrect as it requires an article (e.g., 'a layman') or a plural form.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Option 2 ('using ordinary terms') is semantically correct but lacks the idiomatic precision of the correct answer.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Option 4 ('to ordinary people') would require a change in the sentence structure (explained the phenomenon to ordinary people) and focuses on the audience rather than the style of communication.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                                Additional Information
                                                                                                                                                                                \n
                                                                                                                                                                                  \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • The term layman historically originated from the clergy to distinguish between ordained priests and the laity (the common people). Today, it is used broadly for any non-specialist.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • Using 'layman's terms' often involves the removal of jargon—technical terminology specific to a particular group or occupation.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
                                                                                                                                                                                • In modern usage, gender-neutral alternatives like 'layperson's terms' or 'plain English' are also frequently used to ensure inclusive communication.
                                                                                                                                                                                  • \n
